stemMd: According to the passage, why does a squared beam often give a range of years rather than a single year of felling?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Its ring pattern fits the reference sequence at more than one position.

options.label: B
options.textMd: It comes from an older tree, whose rings are harder to tell apart.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Trees felled in different winters can show identical ring patterns.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Squaring with an axe blurs the pattern of the inner rings, so the beam cannot be matched.

options.label: E
options.textMd: It has usually lost its outer rings, so the felling year has to be estimated from the last surviving ring plus an allowance for the missing sapwood.

explanationMd:
Another **stated-information** question. The answer is in the second paragraph, where the passage explains why "a dated beam does not date a building".

**What to notice first.** The chain of reasoning is given in three short steps: the year of felling is known "only if the outermost ring survives"; "a squared beam has usually lost its outer rings"; so "the last surviving ring gives only a year before which the tree cannot have been felled", and researchers add an allowance for missing sapwood, "which produces a range of years".

**The step that settles it.** The correct choice compresses that chain: outer rings lost, so the felling year must be estimated from the last surviving ring plus an allowance.

**Testing the others.** A pattern that fits at several positions would stop the dating altogether, not widen the felling year. The age of the tree and damage to the inner rings are not mentioned. A repeated pattern from different winters contradicts the bar-code idea.

**How to check.** Read the explanation the passage gives and make sure your choice names the cause it names, not just a plausible-sounding cause.

distractorRationale.a: The passage says a calendar year can be given only when the pattern fits at one position only. A double fit would prevent dating altogether rather than produce a range for the felling year.
distractorRationale.b: The passage says nothing about the age of the tree or the legibility of its rings. Squaring is described as removing wood, not as a property of old trees.
distractorRationale.d: The axe removes the outer rings; the passage does not say it damages the inner ones. In the abbey example, squared beams were dated.
distractorRationale.c: The passage never suggests that different years produce the same pattern. It says the pattern is like a bar code, which is what allows exact placement.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying scientific passage on dating timber by its growth rings. It asks why a squared beam often gives a range of years rather than a single year of felling. Five possible reasons are offered.
